title: LEDA: a Large-Organization Email-Based Decision-Dialogue-Act Analysis Dataset
abstract: Introduces decision-focused dialogue-act annotations over real-world public IETF organizational email and studies automatic tagging of those acts. The dataset is direct evidence for decision-related communicative functions in authentic large-organization email, although it does not by itself provide the full owner, deadline, condition, and exact action-argument schema sought here.
venue: Findings of the Association for Computational Linguistics: ACL 2023

title: Speculation and Negation Scope Detection via Convolutional Neural Networks
abstract: Detects speculation and negation cues together with their scopes using neural models. It offers transfer mechanisms for condition-like uncertainty and negation scope, but it does not evaluate attachment to action arguments in authentic workplace communication.
venue: Proceedings of the 2016 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing

title: Predicate-specific Annotations for Implicit Role Binding: Corpus Annotation, Data Analysis and Evaluation Experiments
abstract: Presents corpus annotation and evaluation for binding implicit semantic roles to non-local discourse entities for selected predicates. It supplies transfer evidence for discourse-level argument recovery, while its domain and predicates differ from workplace task ownership.
venue: Proceedings of the 10th International Conference on Computational Semantics – Short Papers

title: A Two-Step Approach for Implicit Event Argument Detection
abstract: Decomposes implicit event-argument detection into head-word identification followed by expansion to argument spans and evaluates on document-level event data. This is transfer evidence for non-local argument recovery and exact span construction, not direct workplace communication evidence.
venue: Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics

title: Do LLMs suffer from Multi-Party Hangover? A Diagnostic Approach to Addressee Recognition and Response Selection in Conversations
abstract: Diagnoses large-language-model performance on addressee recognition and response selection in multi-party conversations and shows the importance of conversation structure and history. The conversations are not direct authentic workplace-email evidence, so the contribution is transfer evidence for context-dependent participant inference.
venue: Proceedings of the 2024 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing

title: Extraction de tâches dans les e-mails : une approche fondée sur les rôles sémantiques
abstract: Presents a semantic-role-based approach for detecting and structuring tasks in professional email, with roles describing who performs an action, what is done, when, and related participants. This is unusually direct evidence for structured action extraction from workplace email, although the available description does not establish joint annotation of all target slots such as conditions, exceptions, and exact evidence spans.

title: Entity, Relation, and Event Extraction with Contextualized Span Representations
abstract: Presents DyGIE++, a span-based architecture that jointly models entities, relations, and events with contextualized span representations and cross-sentence information. It is transfer evidence for exact trigger and argument span extraction, not a workplace action-item benchmark.
venue: Proceedings of the 2019 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing and the 9th International Joint Conference on Natural Language Processing

title: Decision Detection Using Hierarchical Graphical Models
abstract: Models meeting decision subdialogues with hierarchical graphical models and distinguishes roles such as issues, resolution proposals or restatements, and agreement. This is particularly relevant transfer evidence for separating proposals and agreements around a decision proposition, although it is meeting-domain rather than email/chat evidence.
venue: Proceedings of the 48th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics: Short Papers

title: Event Time Extraction with a Decision Tree of Neural Classifiers
abstract: Models extraction of event times by decomposing temporal anchoring into neural classification decisions. It provides transfer machinery for linking events to time expressions but does not distinguish workplace deadlines from other temporal relations.
venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics

title: Focused Meeting Summarization via Unsupervised Relation Extraction
abstract: Frames decision-focused meeting summarization as relation extraction, separating decision cues from the content associated with them and identifying informative phrases from decision-related utterances. Because the underlying method explicitly relates decision indicators to decision content, it is useful transfer evidence for proposition anchoring and evidence extraction rather than merely generated summarization.
venue: Proceedings of the 13th Annual Meeting of the Special Interest Group on Discourse and Dialogue

title: Classifying Action Items for Semantic Email
abstract: Presents a rule-based system for recognizing email action items such as task assignments and meeting proposals. Its speech-act model structures action items with an Action, an Object, and where applicable a Subject or agent, and distinguishes actions including Request, Assign, Suggest, and Deliver.

title: *SEM 2012 Shared Task: Resolving the Scope and Focus of Negation
abstract: Defines shared tasks for identifying negation cues, their scope, and focus. Scope-sensitive negation is transferable to preventing negated actions from being incorrectly extracted as live requests, commitments, or decisions.

title: Detecting Emails Containing Requests for Action
abstract: Detects email messages containing requests for action and improves classification by first segmenting messages into functional zones and restricting request detection to relevant content. The evaluated target is primarily message-level presence, so it is most useful as act-detection evidence rather than complete action-slot extraction.

title: Detecting Action Items in Multi-party Meetings: Annotation and Initial Experiments
abstract: Defines action items as social actions involving a task description, timeframe, owner, and participant agreement, and introduces a hierarchical utterance-role annotation scheme for the assignment process. It investigates automatic detection while targeting extraction of information useful for reporting and summarization.
venue: Machine Learning for Multimodal Interaction, MLMI 2006

title: Detecting and Summarizing Action Items in Multi-Party Dialogue
abstract: Detects subdialogues in which action items are proposed, discussed, and committed to, then uses semantic parsing to extract phrases that summarize the tasks involved. This directly supports source-grounded extraction rather than unconstrained action-item generation.
venue: 8th SIGdial Workshop on Discourse and Dialogue

title: Shallow Discourse Structure for Action Item Detection
abstract: Uses shallow discourse structure and a hierarchical annotation scheme to detect action-item assignment regions in meeting transcripts. The work explicitly targets properties including responsible party, task, and deadline rather than treating an action item as an isolated sentence label.
venue: Analyzing Conversations in Text and Speech

title: Extracting Decisions from Multi-Party Dialogue Using Directed Graphical Models and Semantic Similarity
abstract: Uses directed graphical models to detect decision discussions and distinguishes dialogue-act roles such as the issue under discussion and its resolution. It also summarizes decisions by extracting phrases from the source dialogue rather than generating unsupported decisions.

title: Meeting Action Item Detection with Regularized Context Modeling
abstract: Introduces a manually annotated Chinese meeting corpus for action-item detection and a Context-Drop method that exploits local and global conversational context with contrastive learning. Experiments cover the new Chinese corpus and the English AMI corpus.

title: Can Requests-for-Action and Commitments-to-Act be Reliably Identified in Email Messages?
abstract: Reports an exploratory annotation study in which human coders label the presence and strength of Requests-for-Action and Commitments-to-Act in workplace email at sentence level. The study establishes empirical annotation evidence for distinguishing requests that impose action on recipients from promises by senders.

title: Requests and Commitments in Email are More Complex Than You Think: Eight Reasons to be Cautious
abstract: Analyzes difficult real-world cases encountered when annotating and extracting workplace-email requests and commitments, identifying eight categories of problematic phenomena and proposing annotation treatments. It is particularly relevant to conditional, repeated, ambiguous, and context-dependent action evidence.

title: The nature of requests and commitments in email messages
abstract: Develops precise utterance-level definitions for requests and commitments in workplace email using speech-act theory and two annotation experiments on Enron email. It explicitly focuses on utterances that place responsibility for action on the sender or recipients and analyzes difficult surface realizations.

title: Using Speech Acts to Categorize Email and Identify Email Genres
abstract: Defines email-oriented speech acts and uses them to characterize communicative purpose and email genres. The contribution is useful as an email speech-act taxonomy and act-detection baseline rather than as a slot extractor.

title: TimeML: Robust Specification of Event and Temporal Expressions in Text
abstract: Defines a markup language for events, temporal expressions, and temporal links that relate events to times and to other events. The event-time relation layer is directly relevant to linking a deadline expression to the action it constrains rather than extracting dates in isolation.

title: Dialogue act modeling for automatic tagging and recognition of conversational speech
abstract: Develops statistical dialogue-act tagging for conversational speech using lexical, prosodic, and discourse-sequence models. It provides transferable methods for modeling contextual dependencies among speech acts, including agreement and action-oriented dialogue functions.

title: On the collective classification of email "speech acts"
abstract: Classifies email messages for email acts such as requests and commitments and exploits sequential dependencies between messages in the same thread using collective classification. It provides useful evidence for contextual speech-act detection but remains primarily message-level classification.

title: Detecting Action-Items in E-mail
abstract: Detects emails that require action or response and, importantly, highlights the specific text expressing the request. The work explicitly contrasts localized action-item detection with whole-message text categorization.

title: The Possible, the Plausible, and the Desirable: Event-Based Modality Detection for Language Processing
abstract: Models modality as a relation between modal expressions and the events they modify, covering a wider range of modal constructions than cue-only classification. The event-scoped representation is useful for distinguishing the status of an action rather than merely detecting a modal word.

title: Learning with Weak Supervision for Email Intent Detection
abstract: Uses user interaction logs as weak supervision for detecting actionable intents in email, combined with clean annotated data and self-paced learning. Experiments cover multiple email intent-detection tasks, including request- and action-related intents. The work provides direct empirical email evidence for communicative intent detection but not structured owner, deadline, or condition arguments.

title: Context-Aware Intent Identification in Email Conversations
abstract: Studies sentence-level intent identification in workplace email using a large publicly available enterprise email dataset and models message and conversational context. The intent taxonomy includes action-relevant categories rather than only broad topical classes, with requests and future-action intents among the studied phenomena. It remains intent classification rather than full argument extraction.

title: Domain Adaptation for Commitment Detection in Email
abstract: Studies detection of commitments to future actions in email and demonstrates substantial domain bias when models are transferred between email corpora. It evaluates feature-level, sample-level, and representation-based domain adaptation for commitment detection. The target is genuine future-action commitment rather than generic modality or capability.

title: Monitoring Commitments in People-Driven Service Engagements
abstract: Models and detects commitments in real-world email and chat service engagements, including commitment creation as well as later delegation, completion, and cancellation. Evaluation uses the Enron email corpus and an HP IT-support chat dataset. The commitment representation captures who is responsible to whom for achieving what, with circumstances as part of the underlying semantics, although the paper does not establish separate field-level accuracy for all such arguments.
venue: 2013 IEEE International Conference on Services Computing

title: Deep Structured Neural Network for Event Temporal Relation Extraction
abstract: Combines a neural pairwise temporal-relation scorer with structured inference enforcing constraints such as temporal transitivity. It is evaluated on multiple event temporal-relation datasets. The work is useful transfer evidence for maintaining consistent action-time relations but does not distinguish task deadlines in workplace communication.

title: The BioScope corpus: biomedical texts annotated for uncertainty, negation and their scopes
abstract: Introduces a corpus with token-level annotations for negation and uncertainty cues and sentence-level annotations of their linguistic scopes. Independent annotators and adjudication were used to construct the resource. This is transfer evidence for linking negation or uncertainty cues to the textual material they govern, not direct evidence for negated workplace obligations.

title: Lin: Unsupervised Extraction of Tasks from Textual Communication
abstract: Studies extraction of specific tasks expressed through commitments and requests in emails and chat messages. Lin is an unsupervised approach based on dependency parsing and VerbNet and is evaluated across domains, including unseen domains. The work extracts task content rather than only predicting whether a message is actionable.

title: Assigning people to tasks identified in email: The EPA dataset for addressee tagging for detected task intent
abstract: Introduces the Enron People Assignment dataset, in which tasks described in authentic workplace emails are associated with the person or people responsible for carrying them out. The paper identifies both tasks and responsible people, defines evaluation methods, and evaluates a model against baselines. This is direct evidence for action-specific owner or assignee extraction.

title: Prompt for Extraction? PAIE: Prompting Argument Interaction for Event Argument Extraction
abstract: Presents an extractive event-argument model with role-specific span selectors and multi-role prompts so interactions among arguments are modeled jointly. Bipartite matching supports optimal span assignment, and the method can extract multiple arguments sharing the same role at sentence and document level. It is strong transfer evidence for action-specific span binding when several arguments coexist, but it is not a workplace obligation benchmark.

title: A Modality Lexicon and its use in Automatic Tagging
abstract: Defines a modality annotation scheme centered on three linked components: modality trigger, target, and holder, and develops a modality lexicon plus automatic taggers. The explicit trigger-to-target representation is relevant to attaching modal meaning to the correct action rather than assigning only a sentence-level modality label. It is transfer evidence and does not specifically establish workplace commitment extraction.

title: Fine-Grained Analysis of Team Collaborative Dialogue
abstract: Develops fine-grained dialogue analysis for authentic organizational Slack conversations in a software-development setting. The hierarchical annotation scheme includes collaborative acts such as proposals, requests, assignments, and rejections, and the work evaluates a transformer-plus-CRF architecture using long-range context. It is direct enterprise-chat evidence for distinguishing several action and decision-related communicative acts, although it is not a complete structured action benchmark.

title: Explicit, Implicit, and Scattered: Revisiting Event Extraction to Capture Complex Arguments
abstract: Introduces DiscourseEE, an event-extraction dataset with explicit, implicit, and scattered event arguments, showing that important arguments may require contextual inference or evidence distributed across a document. The dataset contains 7,464 argument annotations from online health discourse. It is transfer evidence for implicit and non-contiguous action arguments rather than direct workplace communication evidence.
